This early life stage is energetically dependent entirely upon endogenous yolk reserves, and the newly emerged prolarva, still carrying a prominent yolk sac, initiates its transition to exogenous feeding only after mouth opening and yolk-sac resorption are complete. The species, belonging to the family Sparidae, is widely distributed across the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic, where it occupies coastal rocky reefs and seagrass meadows, and its reproductive strategy is tuned to seasonal environmental cues that optimise larval survival.

Field-based studies employing mark-recapture techniques and otolith increment analysis have provided robust estimates of the species' growth trajectory and asymptotic size. Sexual maturation in White sea bream is attained at a specific body length threshold rather than at a fixed age, a pattern common among sparids. The total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonad maturation and gametogenesis, is 17 centimeters [Lp = 17 centimeters], a size at which individuals first become capable of contributing to the reproductive population. This length-based maturity schedule allows the species to buffer against interannual variability in growth rates driven by temperature and food availability. Lifespan and actuarial senescence patterns for Diplodus sargus have been characterised through long-term tagging programs and catch curve analysis. Under the environmental conditions prevailing across much of its range, where mean annual water temperatures approximate 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is 3650 days [am = 3650 days], which places White sea bream among the longer-lived members of the genus within the Sparidae family. This longevity is notable among coastal sparids and positions the species as a relatively long-lived, iteroparous strategist that spreads its reproductive effort across multiple seasons. The extended adult phase allows individuals to achieve the large body sizes documented earlier and to contribute numerous spawning batches over consecutive years. Natural mortality in older adults has been linked to the progressive deterioration of physiological functions, including reduced swimming performance and diminished immunological competence, which render senescent individuals more susceptible to predation and parasitic infestation. Comparative data from congeneric species, such as Diplodus puntazzo, suggest that these longevity estimates are consistent within the genus, although local oceanographic conditions may modulate the realised lifespan in different populations.

Comparative life-history analyses situate White sea bream as a moderately fast-growing, medium-sized iteroparous fish with a clear trade-off between early reproduction and continued somatic investment. The rapid embryogenesis quantified at 4 days [ab = 4 days] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], while brief, typifies the warm-water teleost pattern, and contrasts sharply with the prolonged planktonic larval duration of several weeks that follows. The ultimate total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters] places the species at an intermediate position within the Sparidae family, larger than many small-bodied Diplodus species but smaller than the massive Dentex dentex. The asymptotic wet weight of 1900 grams [Wwi = 1900 grams] is consistent with this body size, and the puberty length threshold of 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm] ensures that individuals begin reproducing at roughly 38% of their ultimate length, a life-history strategy that balances the risks of delayed maturity against the fecundity benefits of larger body size. Population models incorporating these demographic parameters indicate that the species can sustain moderate fishing pressure, though careful management of the spawning stock is necessary to maintain recruitment success in exploited regions.
